Acute Subclavian Artery Thrombosis

Hand · 1 / 103

1Basics

Epidemiology & risk factors

Definitionacute UE ischaemia from proximal occlusion at subclavian artery level

Incidencerare, <1%

Risk factorsaortic arch abnormality, aortic arch syndrome, trauma, arterial catheterisation, pre-existing stenosis/atheroma at subclavian ostium

Patternsslow occlusion (atherosclerosis) · blue finger syndrome (repeated microemboli) · acute global ischaemia (large emboli)

Anatomy

Left subclavian3rd branch of aortic arch

Right subclavianbranch of brachiocephalic (innominate) artery

Vertebral arteriesarise from subclavian → join as basilar → cerebellum → risk of vertebrobasilar insufficiency / basilar stroke

2Mechanism

Commonest cause of UE thromboembolismatrial fibrillation (80% of UE thromboembolism)

Cardiac embolismup to 93% of acute UE ischaemia; AF → loss of atrial contraction → stasis → thrombus

Other cardiac sourcescardiomyopathy, valvular disease, ASD, aortic arch abnormality; endocarditis → septic emboli

Hand arterial occlusion (general)usually post-traumatic ulnar artery; venous occlusion → hypercoagulable state

3Presentation

Historysudden onset, no inciting event

Symptomsarm pain, paraesthesia, nausea, exertional pain/fatigue

Examcyanotic/pale, cold limb; pulses absent (axillary, brachial, radial, ulnar); neuro exam often normal

Non-occlusivepulses absent but Doppler signal present (monophasic)

BPdiffers between arms

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Modality Fact
Arteriography Recommended diagnostic test; allows percutaneous treatment at same sitting
CT angiography Fast; rules out other causes
MRA cannot treat at diagnosis
Doppler US Signal may persist in non-occlusive disease
Echocardiography Rules out cardiac embolus after treatment

Labs

Hypercoagulable panelrule out underlying disorder; labs usually unremarkable

5Management

Acute subclavian thrombosis
  • Symptomatic limb ischaemia→percutaneous or open revascularisation
    • percutaneous→thrombolysis / PTA / aspiration / stent
    • open→embolectomy-thrombectomy / bypass
  • Adjunct (all)→IV + oral anticoagulation

Arterial thromboembolism – treatment & anticoagulation

Percutaneousintra-arterial thrombolysis, PTA, manual aspiration, stenting (protect vertebral artery with balloon)

Openembolectomy/thrombectomy, bypass grafting

Medicalheparin, aspirin, clopidogrel, IV thrombolysis, GP IIb/IIIa antagonists; limited role alone if limb-threatening

✗ Wrong option: aortic root replacementfor ascending thoracic aortic dissection, not subclavian disease

AF prophylaxisanticoagulants
✗ Wrong options: antiplatelets = mechanical valves · statin = ischaemic cardiomyopathy · antibiotics = endocarditis · β-blocker = rate only

AF anticoagulation (AHA/ACC/HRS 2014) Factors
High risk (any 1 → anticoagulate) Prior stroke/TIA, systemic thromboembolism, age ≥75
Moderate (>1 → anticoagulate) Age 65–74, ♀, HTN, DM, heart failure, arterial disease

6Complications

Limb ischaemiagangrene, limb loss; delayed diagnosis → amputation

Basilar strokeprolonged ischaemia, or iatrogenic emboli if vertebrobasilar system unprotected during endovascular Rx

Prognosisfavourable with prompt Rx; untreated → stroke + amputation

How it's asked

"Absent pulses + Doppler signal — treatment EXCEPT"aortic root replacement
✗ Wrong options: thrombolysis, PTA, aspiration, stent

"Best diagnostic test"arteriography (diagnose + treat)

"Commonest cause of UE thromboembolism"atrial fibrillation

"AF patient — reduce hand thromboembolism"anticoagulants

"Feared complication of delay / endovascular Rx"basilar stroke

AIN Compressive Neuropathy

Hand · 2 / 103

1Basics

Epidemiology & aetiology

EponymKiloh-Nevin syndrome = AIN compression (TO) (✗ Wrong options: PIN compression (TO))

Incidencerare; <1% of median neuropathies

Commonest causetransient neuritis (Parsonage-Turner); non-traumatic AIN palsy usually = neuritis (viral, autoimmune)

Parsonage-Turnerviral brachial neuritis → bilateral AIN signs (TO); preceded by intense shoulder pain + viral prodrome

Compression sitesdeep head of pronator teres (most common anatomical, TO) · FDS arch (TO) · edge of lacertus fibrosus (TO) · Gantzer's muscle = accessory head FPL (TO) · thrombosed radial/ulnar/AI artery · accessory FDS→FDP muscle · FCRB, palmaris profundus

Surgical finding (Park)commonest compressive structure at exploration = fibrous band of FDS; 4/11 had no compression

AIN motor distribution (FPL, FDP index)

Originterminal motor branch of median n.; ~4 cm distal to medial epicondyle (Orthobullets) · 5–8 cm distal to lateral epicondyle (OB/Orthobullets); dorsoradial aspect of median n.

Coursebetween FDS & FDP → between FPL & FDP → on interosseous membrane with AI artery → pronator quadratus → wrist capsule (radiocarpal, intercarpal, DRUJ)

Innervates (3)FPL · FDP index + middle · pronator quadratus

Sensorynone cutaneous (articular branches only)

Not AINpronator teres (median, before AIN leaves) · FCR (median) · FCU (ulnar) · FDB (foot, medial plantar)

Martin-Gruber anastomosis

MGAmotor connection median/AIN → ulnar in proximal 1/3 forearm; sensory spared; most common forearm anomalous innervation

Prevalence15% (Orthobullets) · 15–40% (OB) · pooled 19.5%, 57.6% from AIN (meta-analysis); more often right

Suppliesadductor pollicis + dorsal interossei (intrinsics) → complete AIN palsy may show intrinsic weakness

High ulnar laceration + intrinsics workMartin-Gruber

MGA type IImost common; median fibres → 1st dorsal interosseous → median laceration = median deficit + cannot abduct index; ulnar sensation preserved

MGA II on NCSusually normal (1st DI not routinely tested) → careful exam

Anastomosis Site Direction Clue / prevalence
Martin-Gruber Forearm Median/AIN → ulnar (motor) High ulnar cut, intrinsics work · median cut, no index abduction
Marinacci Forearm Ulnar → median ("reverse MG") Rarest (0.7% / 4%); proximal median lesion with APB/thenar preserved
Riche-Cannieu Hand Recurrent median ↔ deep ulnar (motor ± sensory) 55%; preserved thenar function; "all-ulnar hand"
Berrettini Hand Common digital nn. (3rd–4th), sensory >80%; injured at CTR → ↓ 3rd web sensation; no motor

Not median–ulnarLinburg-Comstock = FPL–FDP index tendinous connection · anconeus epitrochlearis = cubital tunnel compression

3Presentation

Hallmarkmotor deficit without sensory loss (TO); normal median sensory exam

OK signcannot make OK sign = Kiloh-Nevin sign (TO) → weak thumb IP flexion (FPL) + index DIP flexion (FDP)

Painvague deep forearm pain, often absent; if present lasts 2–3 wk

PQ testweak resisted pronation with elbow maximally flexed (neutralises pronator teres)

Tenodesisintact tenodesis = tendons intact → distinguishes from FPL attritional rupture (RA)

Severeforearm atrophy

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisclinical + EMG/NCS

Key radiology findings

MRIif mass suspected; T2/STIR ↑ signal FPL, FDP, PQ → PQ oedema = most reliable

EMGfibrillations, positive sharp waves in FPL + FDP index/middle; rules out proximal lesion, grades severity, tracks recovery

Differentialsflexor tendon rupture · proximal lesion (C-spine, plexus) · pronator syndrome · CTS · conversion disorder (not if objective EMG findings)

5Management

AIN palsy
  • No mass / no trauma→OBSERVATION, rest, PT (12 mo)
    • no recovery at 12 mo→SURGICAL DECOMPRESSION
  • Space-occupying mass→DECOMPRESSION + excision
  • Penetrating injury→EXPLORE + primary repair

AIN syndrome – diagnosis & observation (neuritis)

First lineobservation, rest, PT in all without a mass; treatment mostly non-surgical (TO); splinting at 90° (Rodner) · massage, forearm stretches

Recoverybegins 3–12 mo; full by 18 mo (mean ~9 mo) → "gradual improvement over 1 y" · "persistent sx <2 y then spontaneous resolution"

Better prognosisage <40 (faster recovery)

Not indicatedsteroid injection (no data) · CTR · early tendon/nerve transfer

Operative criteria

Indication Threshold
Clear space-occupying mass Early decompression
Failed nonop 12 mo (Orthobullets, Chi & Harness) · 6 mo in complete palsy (Sood & Burke)
Penetrating injury Explore + end-to-end repair
Age <40 Surgery controversial (uniform nonop response)

Surgical success~75%

Decompressionlazy-S proximal volar forearm; release superficial head PT, lacertus fibrosus, FDS arch, Gantzer's, ligate crossing vessels; elbow ROM day 2

6Complications

Persistent AIN deficitrare (~5–10 cases) → tendon transfer: brachioradialis → FPL

X vs Y

AIN syndrome Pronator syndrome PIN syndrome FPL rupture
Sensory Normal Radial 3½ + thenar Normal Normal
Motor FPL, FDP-I/M, PQ ± Thumb extension/retropulsion, finger ext FPL only
Pain Absent / 2–3 wk Proximal forearm Lateral elbow —
Tenodesis Intact Intact Intact Lost
Release Gantzer's, FDS arch Lacertus fibrosus Arcade of Frohse —

How it's asked

"Kiloh-Nevin — all true EXCEPT"compression of PIN (TO)

"Parsonage-Turner + weak pronation, no sensory loss"AIN syndrome → observation
✗ Wrong options: Gantzer release

"Fibs in FPL + FDP-I after flu, no numbness — next step?"observation, improves over 1 y

"Weak thumb IP flexion, normal 2PD, normal MRI — course?"resolves spontaneously <2 y

"Stab proximal forearm, no index DIP flexion — what else fails?"FPL
✗ Wrong options: pronator teres, FCR

"High ulnar laceration, intrinsics still work"Martin-Gruber

"Antecubital laceration, median deficit + no index abduction"Martin-Gruber type II

"Most reliable MRI sign"PQ oedema

"Persistent AIN palsy — transfer?"brachioradialis → FPL

Apert Syndrome

Hand · 3 / 103

1Basics

FGFR2 mutation & clinical features

Synonymacrocephalosyndactyly type 1: cranium + hands + feet

Incidencerare; 1/80,000 live births

Featuresbilateral complex syndactyly hands & feet (index, middle, ring most affected) · symphalangism · craniosynostosis → flat skull, broad forehead (acrocephaly) · hypertelorism · glenoid hypoplasia · radioulnar synostosis

Cognitionnormal → moderately disabled

Feetpredictable dysmorphism + progressive fusions through skeletal maturity

Genes & lab markers

Gene Condition
FGFR2 Apert (AD, most new cases sporadic)
✗ Wrong option: FGFR3 Achondroplasia
✗ Wrong option: COL2A1 (chr 12) SED congenita
✗ Wrong option: SEDL X-linked SED tarda
✗ Wrong option: fibrillin Marfan
✗ Wrong option: SHH Radial longitudinal deficiency (TAR, Holt-Oram, VACTERL)
✗ Wrong option: PMP22 Charcot-Marie-Tooth
✗ Wrong option: COL1A1 Osteogenesis imperfecta

3Presentation

Facedysmorphic, flattened features, wide-set eyes

Rosebud handcomplex syndactyly; index, middle, ring share a common nail

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-raycomplex syndactyly (bony fusion of central digits)

5Management

Apert hand
  • ~1 y→release BORDER digits
  • ~1.5 y → digit reconstruction: central 3→2 digits

How it's asked

"Gene in Apert?"FGFR2
✗ Wrong options: FGFR3, COL2A1, SEDL, fibrillin

"Flat face + wide-set eyes + fused fingers"Apert
✗ Wrong options: MED, cleidocranial, Noonan, achondroplasia

"Infant rosebud hands — mutation?"FGFR2
✗ Wrong options: SHH, PMP22, COL1A1

"Digits most affected"index, middle, ring

Atypical Mycobacterium Infections

Hand · 4 / 103

1Basics

Epidemiology & organisms

Incidencerare; 0.05 / 100,000 / y

Whomarine workers, fishermen; immunocompromised host (most have some immunosuppression)

Sitehand & wrist in 50%

Incubationavg 2 wk (up to 6 mo); time to diagnosis often >1 y (missed Dx)

Prior steroid injectionpoorer outcome

Organism Habitat Culture
M. marinum Most common; stagnant fresh/salt water, aquariums, fish nets Löwenstein-Jensen at 30–32 °C
M. kansasii Soil —
M. terrae Soil 37 °C
M. avium intracellulare Terminal AIDS (also non-HIV) Room temperature

Mycobacterium marinum

Classicfisherman/aquarium cut → dorsal hand swelling weeks later → grows on Löwenstein-Jensen at 30 °C after ~2 wk → M. marinum

Other aquatic pathogensVibrio spp., Aeromonas hydrophila

Fishmonger's disease (erysipeloid)

Organisms (TO)commonest: Streptococcus iniae, Vibrio vulnificus, M. marinum · others: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, Aeromonas hydrophila, Vibrio damsela, Proteus vulgaris, Morganella morganii, Lactococcus garvieae, M. abscessus, Streptococcus halichoeri

Mechanism (TO)penetration by sharp instruments or fish bony spines; immunosuppressed → high morbidity & mortality

NOT a cause (TO)Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Compound palmar ganglion (TB tenosynovitis)

Definition (TO)tuberculous tenosynovitis of wrist/hand flexor tendons; radial + ulnar bursae

Shape (TO)hourglass / dumb-bell swelling proximal & distal to flexor retinaculum (across wrist crease) → positive cross-fluctuation

Bursal anatomy (TO)ulnar bursa communicates with radial bursa in 80% → horseshoe tenosynovitis

Spread (TO)little finger → ulnar bursa → Parona's space (more commonly associated) · thumb → radial → ulnar bursa

Causes (TO)TB (commonest comorbidity) · RA · infection · SLE · gout · PVNS of tendon sheath · fungal

NOT a cause (TO)malignancy

Diagnosis (TO)clinical, always confirmed by histopathology

Treatment (TO)progresses to gross destruction → excision without delay

3Presentation

Earlypapules, ulcers, nodules on hand; cutaneous rash; often single nodule → lymphatic spread

Latetenosynovitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis

Look-alikeindistinguishable from TB infection

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisclinical + culture (cultures & sensitivities = key)

Histologygranulomas ± acid-fast bacilli on AFB stain

CultureLöwenstein-Jensen; M. marinum 30–32 °C · MAI room temp · M. terrae 37 °C

Differentialsherpetic whitlow, fungal infection, psoriasis

5Management

Atypical mycobacterial hand infection
  • Early (papules / nodules)→ORAL ANTIMYCOBACTERIALS
    • osteomyelitis→ADD RIFAMPIN
  • Late (tenosynovitis / joint / bone)→DEBRIDEMENT + combination Abx 3–6 mo

Oral agentsethambutol, tetracycline, TMP-SMX, clarithromycin, azithromycin; + rifampin if osteomyelitis

Mortality32% with sepsis / untreated

X vs Y

Organism Classic exposure
M. marinum Fish nets, aquarium; LJ 30 °C
M. terrae Soil; 37 °C
Sporothrix schenckii Thorn (rose gardener) — fungus
Bartonella henselae Cat scratch; epitrochlear lymphadenopathy; endocarditis
Eikenella corrodens Human bite; Gram −ve
Erysipelothrix / S. iniae / Vibrio Fishmonger's disease

How it's asked

"Fisherman cut, LJ medium at 30 °C"M. marinum
✗ Wrong options: M. terrae, Sporothrix, Bartonella, Eikenella

"MAI culture temperature"room temperature

"Add for osteomyelitis"rifampin

"Fishmonger's disease NOT caused by"Pseudomonas aeruginosa (TO)

"Compound palmar ganglion — true"more commonly with little finger infection (TO)

"Dumb-bell wrist swelling, cross-fluctuation — comorbidity?"tuberculosis (TO)

"Compound palmar ganglion NOT seen in"malignancy (TO)

Base of Thumb Fractures

Hand · 5 / 103

1Basics

Epidemiology & anatomy

Incidence80% of thumb fractures involve the MC base; commonest pattern = extra-articular epibasal

CMC jointsaddle-shaped, trapezium + 1st MC base; flex–ext ~53°, abd–add ~42°, very limited axial rotation

Volar beak ligament= anterior oblique ligament (AOL); trapezial tuberosity → volar edge 1st MC → keeps volar-ulnar Bennett fragment attached to trapezium

Dorsoradial ligamentdorsoradial trapezial tubercle → dorsal MC base; important for CMC stability but does not hold Bennett fragment

Do not hold the fragmentanterior/posterior intermetacarpal ligaments (no trapezial attachment), posterior oblique ligament

Deforming forces (APL, adductor pollicis, EPL) & reduction manoeuvre

Muscle Nerve Pull on shaft fragment
Abductor pollicis longus (main force, TO) PIN Proximal, dorsal, radial
Adductor pollicis Ulnar Supination + adduction (ulnar angulation)
Extensor pollicis longus PIN Proximal, dorsal, radial; adds ulnar angulation (less important)
EPB PIN Small contribution

Primary deforming pairAPL + adductor pollicis (OB, TO) · three-muscle answer = APL + AdP + EPL (Orthobullets) — read the options

Nerves of deforming musclesulnar + PIN
✗ Wrong options: AIN · recurrent median

Not deformingAPB, FPB, opponens (thenar, recurrent median), FPL, PQ, brachioradialis (distal radius)

Shaft displacement (TO)Bennett: shaft lateral, proximal, dorsal; Rolando: diaphyseal fragment usually not displaced

Reduction manoeuvrelongitudinal traction + palmar abduction + pronation + pressure on MC base

2Mechanism

Mechanismaxial load on partially flexed (adducted) thumb, e.g. clenched-fist punch (TO)

Pathoanatomyimperfect reduction → ↑ joint contact pressure → early arthritis; excessive angulation → MCP hyperextension deformity (malunion)

3Presentation

Findingsbase-of-thumb pain, swelling, ecchymosis, CMC tenderness, painful ROM

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsRoberts view (true AP: full pronation, dorsum of thumb on cassette) + true lateral (hand pronated 30°, beam 15° distal) + oblique

Best view30° pronated view

Bennettsmall MC base fragment still articulating with trapezium

RolandoY sign = base split into volar + dorsal fragments

Traction viewRolando / comminuted pattern

CTcomplex patterns, fragment detail

Classification of 1st MC base fractures

Type Description Image
Extra-articular oblique Oblique line, joint spared
Extra-articular transverse Transverse line, joint spared
Bennett Partial intra-articular, palmar-ulnar fragment; oblique fracture-dislocation
Rolando Complete intra-articular, Y / T / V-shaped, 3-part (TO)
Comminuted Severely comminuted complete intra-articular

Rolando (TO)intra-articular fracture base 1st MC
✗ Wrong options: extra-articular · "adductor longus" · commonest thumb fracture-dislocation

Treatment criteria

Pattern Accept / nonop Operate
Extra-articular <30° angulation after CR >30° or can't hold in spica → CRPP
Bennett <1 mm step-off / displacement >1 mm → CRPP or ORIF
Rolando — <1 mm → CRPP; >1 mm → ORIF / ex-fix; comminution dictates strategy

Open reduction threshold>1 mm displacement (Orthobullets, Soyer) · >2 mm step-off despite CR (Carlsen) — read the options

5Management

1st MC base fracture
  • Extra-articular <30°→CR + thumb spica
    • >30° / lost reduction→CRPP
  • Bennett / Rolando ≤1 mm→spica (Bennett) / CRPP (Rolando)
  • >1 mm displaced
    • large fragments→ORIF (screws / T-plate)
    • small fragments→CRPP
    • soft-tissue injury / too small / impacted→distraction ex-fix

NonopCR (traction, palmar abduction, pronation) + thumb spica; >3 wk old with no motion at fracture → accept step-off + cast

Small avulsion (TO)CR + thumb spica 6 wk; unstable → closed/open reduction + K-wires + spica 4–6 wk (TO)

CRPPtransverse extra-articular → transarticular K-wire; oblique → intermetacarpal K-wire; risk loss of reduction

ORIFvolar Gedda–Moberg approach; thenar reflected, longitudinal capsulotomy; screws or T-plate; risk SBRN injury, wound problems if oedema

Ex-fixtwo 3 mm pins dorsoradial MC + two in radius ± 2nd MC; risk pin-site infection

Key outcome factoranatomic articular congruity > fixation method; reduction predicts radiographic arthritis
✗ Wrong options: symptomatic

6Complications

Post-traumatic CMC arthritisrisk ↑ with comminution, major step-off, multiple small fragments

MalunionMCP hyperextension deformity, long-term disability

Poor prognosisBennett, Rolando, comminuted, delayed treatment · good: acute, extra-articular

X vs Y

Bennett Rolando
Articular Partial intra-articular Complete intra-articular
Shape Oblique, single volar-ulnar fragment Y / T / V, volar + dorsal fragments
Held by AOL (volar beak) AOL holds volar fragment
Shaft Displaced proximal/dorsal/radial Usually not displaced (TO)
X-ray sign Fragment stays with trapezium Y sign

How it's asked

"Primary deforming forces on Bennett / Rolando?"APL + adductor pollicis
✗ Wrong options: adductor pollicis longus + abductor pollicis

"Three deforming muscles overcome by reduction?"APL, adductor pollicis, EPL
✗ Wrong options: APB · brachioradialis

"Nerves to the deforming muscles?"ulnar + PIN
✗ Wrong options: AIN · recurrent median

"Structure holding fragment to trapezium?"anterior oblique (volar beak) ligament
✗ Wrong options: dorsoradial · intermetacarpal · posterior oblique

"Reduction manoeuvre?"traction + palmar abduction + pronation

"True of Rolando?"intra-articular fracture base 1st MC (TO)

"Best radiographic view?"30° pronated true lateral / Roberts view

Basilar Thumb Arthritis

Hand · 6 / 103

1Basics

Epidemiology

Frequency in handDIP > thumb CMC > PIP > MCP (2nd most common hand OA)

Whopostmenopausal ♀, Caucasian; 40% ♀ / 25% ♂ >75 y

Second patient groupyoung manual labourer, post-traumatic (old intra-articular #) → fusion candidate

AssociatedCTS in up to 50% · MCP hyperextension · STT OA (62% at trapeziectomy)

Anatomy

Jointtrapeziometacarpal (TMC) = biconcave saddle; CMC joint reactive force = 13× pinch force

Anterior oblique (volar beak) ligprimary stabiliser vs subluxation; palmar tubercle trapezium → ulnar MC base; its attenuation = cause of OA

Dorsoradial ligstrongest/thickest; primary restraint to dorsal dislocation

Intermetacarpal lig2nd MC base → 1st MC base; restrains radial translation

FCRruns in palmar groove of trapezium (used in LRTI)

2Mechanism

Beak lig attenuation → dorsoradial subluxation of MC base → cartilage wear

Z (zig-zag) deformitypainful abduction avoided → MC adduction + palmar flexion → 1st web contracture → compensatory MCP hyperextension (EPB pull) → ± IP flexion

NOT a sequelaCMC extension deformity (EXCEPT question)

Why MCP hyperext mattersleft untreated → deforming force → recurrent MC subluxation after CMC surgery

3Presentation

Historypain at thumb base, ↓ pinch/grip, worse opening jars, key pinch

ExamTTP over CMC · grind test (axial load + circumduction) · shear test (circumduction + translation) · crepitus

Late signsMC adduction, 1st web contracture, fixed MCP hyperextension (Z)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Finding / view Fact asked
Roberts view True AP of TMC: thumb flat, hyperpronated, beam on trapezium
Standard series AP + lateral hand
OA signs Joint space narrowing, sclerosis, osteophytes (<2 mm = II, >2 mm = III), dorsoradial subluxation of MC base
STT involvement = Eaton IV (pantrapezial) → contraindicates CMC fusion

Extensor tendon injury
  • Laceration <50% + can extend against resistance→PROTECTED EARLY MOTION
  • Laceration >50% (any zone)→TENDON REPAIR
  • Closed injury→SPLINT the joint of the zone
    • Zone I mallet→DIP extension splint 6 wk
    • Zone III central slip→PIP extension splint, DIP free
    • Zone V sagittal band→MCP extension splint 4-6 wk

Situation Treatment
Laceration >50% width Repair
Bony mallet + P3 volar subluxation CRPP through DIP / extension-block pinning; ORIF if >50% articular surface

Chronic / irreparable Reconstruction (2-stage)
Chronic EPL rupture EIP → EPL transfer

Mallet (zone I) splinting

DIP extension splintacute (<12 wk), nondisplaced bony mallet, chronic (>12 wk) if supple + congruent; full-time 6 wk + part-time 4–6 wk; avoid hyperextension (skin necrosis); keep PIP free; noncompliance common

Central slip injury – Elson test & PIP extension splinting

Why DIP motionprevents oblique retinacular ligament contracture / adhesions

Strengthnumber of strands crossing repair > grasping loops; 4–6 strands → early active motion; epitendinous optional

1Basics

Pulley anatomy – annular/cruciform sequence, A2 & A4, thumb oblique pulley

Finger sequenceA1, A2, C1, A3, C2, A4, C3 (prox → distal); 5 annular + 3 cruciate

Joint pulleysA1, A3, A5 → arise from palmar plates of MCP, PIP, DIP

Bone pulleysA2 = periosteum proximal half of proximal phalanx · A4 = midportion of middle phalanx

Most importantA2 + A4 → prevent bowstringing; minimum to preserve/reconstruct in flexor tendon surgery

Ideala pulley proximal and distal to each joint; preserve/reconstruct ≥3 pulleys

Cruciate (C1–C3)thin, collapsible; prevent sheath collapse/expansion; let annular pulleys approximate in flexion

Trigger fingerA1 most commonly involved

Thumb pulleys

Thumb sequenceA1 – Av – oblique – A2 (2 annular + Av + oblique)

Oblique pulleymost important in thumb; analogue of finger C1 position; full FPL excursion, prevents bowstringing

Oblique originproximal half of proximal phalanx (Orthobullets) · ulnar side of PP base → radial side of DP base, 4 mm wide (Bayat, OB)

A1 (thumb)at MCP volar plate; ~6 mm; radial digital nerve closest (2.7 mm) · ulnar 5.4 mm

A2 (thumb)5–10 mm (Orthobullets) · 8 mm (Bayat); contributes least to arc of motion

Bowstringing ruleif A2 intact, cutting A1 OR oblique alone → no bowstringing; cutting both A1 + oblique → bowstringing

Restore kinematics (A2 intact)repair oblique OR A1

Bayat caveatonce A1 + Av both cut, oblique can no longer prevent bowstringing

Av pulley type Image Feature
I Transverse, parallel to A1, gap to A1
II No gap to A1
III Triangular/oblique, fibres converge radially

2Mechanism

Pulley rupture – climbers, grading & sequelae

Mechanismextending force on flexed (crimped) digit: rock climbers, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, baseball, lifting crimped; or laceration

Climbers75% get UE injury; 30–50% of these = closed pulley injury

Thumb pulley rupturerare; e.g. after steroid injection for FPL tenosynovitis → pain, clicking, ↓ ROM

Sequential ruptures needed for bowstringing; isolated rupture → early functional rehab

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Closed injuryMRI or US to diagnose

MRI signvolar subluxation of flexor tendon (FPL) away from phalanx (normally apposed)

Clinicalvisible bowstringing; FPL intact (bowstringing needs tendon fixed at both ends → not FPL avulsion)

Schöffl classification

Grade Injury Treatment
I Pulley strain Nonop
II Complete rupture A4 or partial A2/A3 Nonop, taping
III Complete rupture A2 or A3 Nonop
IV Multiple ruptures (A2/A3, A2/A3/A4) or single A2/A3 + lumbrical/collateral lig trauma Surgical reconstruction

Outcome (Schöffl)92% nonop returned to previous climbing level

Pulley injury
  • Grade I–III→NONOP (taping, functional rehab)
  • Grade IV→PULLEY RECONSTRUCTION (not repair)
    • A2 (proximal phalanx)→3 LOOPS around bone, DEEP to extensor

Pulley reconstruction

Goalprevent bowstringing → flexion contracture & ↓ ROM; preserve/reconstruct ≥3 pulleys, A2 important; A4 may be sacrificed acutely (unclear)

Thumbreconstruct oblique pulley alone = enough (tendon graft)

First stepexcise all scar dorsal to flexor tendon

Graftextensor retinaculum (synovialised → least gliding resistance) · excised tendon · PL/plantaris · FDS · allograft

Technique Examples Note
Around-the-bone (encircling) Bunnell single loop · Okutsu triple loop Biomechanically strongest (triple loop)
Non-encircling Kleinert ever-present rim · Karev belt loop · Lister extensor retinaculum · Doyle-Blythe PL through volar plate · Pulvertaft weave Weaker

Hemostasisprevents adhesions; check excursion after reconstruction

Effect Cause

Quadriga FDP repaired short → flexor lag of adjacent digits

Flexor tendon laceration

Operative criteria

Situation Criterion → action
Partial laceration <60%, no trigger → no repair · 60–75% or ≥50% + trigger → epitendinous · >75% → repair
Complete laceration Core (4–6 strands for early active motion) + running epitendinous
Timing Within 3 wk (2 wk ideal); FDP avulsion past ~3 wk → retracted; >6 wk pulleys collapse
Re-rupture Scar <1 cm → resect + repair · >1 cm → graft (1-stage if sheath intact, 2-stage if collapsed)
Reconstruction Supple skin, sensate digit, vascularity, full passive ROM
Single-stage graft Pristine sheath + full ROM
Tenolysis >3 mo, stable soft tissue, full passive ROM, active ≪ passive
Immobilise (✗ Wrong options: early motion) Children, non-compliant

Anaesthesialidocaine + adrenaline tumescent; no tourniquet, no sedation

Frostbite

Hand · 35 / 103

1Basics

Epidemiology & risk factors

Demographics♂:♀ 10:1; 30–50 y; homeless, outdoor workers

Distributionupper limb 20% · lower limb 47% · both 30% · head/face 3%

Most important host riskalcohol abuse (63% of admissions); homelessness

Other hostmental illness, PVD, neuropathy, DM, malnutrition, chronic illness, prior cold injury, African descent (Caucasians better cold-induced vasodilatation)

Smoking↓ NO + ↑ fibrinogen/platelets → thrombosis

Environmental factor Threshold
Temperature Risk low > −10°C; high < −25°C
Wind at −18°C Freeze in 1 h at 10 mph · 10 min at 40 mph
Altitude >17,000 ft
Contact Water, ice, metal (↑ severity)

Spectrum of cold injury

Injury Key features
Frostnip Mildest; superficial skin only, no dermal damage; reversible
Chilblain (pernio) Nonfreezing, dry; burning, pruritus; resolves 2 wk; chronic vasculitis in young/middle-aged ♀
Trench (immersion) foot Nonfreezing, wet, <10°C; military
Frostbite Freezing → tissue necrosis → amputation
Hypothermia Core temp ↓; can be fatal

2Mechanism

Limb phase Events
I Cooling/freezing Vasoconstriction → "hunting response" (cyclic AV shunting q10 min); intracellular ice → membrane rupture; extracellular ice → sludging + intracellular dehydration
II Rewarming Crystals melt; endothelium permeable → blisters/oedema; avoid refreezing
III Progressive injury Inflammation, thrombosis, necrosis; ↓ PGE2; ↑ PGF2α + thromboxane B2
IV Resolution Healing ± sequelae or gangrene

Numberssensory nerve dysfunction −10°C; extracellular ice −2 to −15°C

HypothermiaCBT <35°C; shivering stops at 30–32°C → rigidity, mimics death → "no one is dead until warm and dead"

3Presentation

Hypothermia gradesmild 32–35°C · moderate 28–32°C · severe <28°C; brady, AF/VF, resp acidosis, coma

Blistersform 6–24 h after rewarming; degree only defined after rewarming

Severe hand injury signsno Doppler signal, absent cap refill, dark purple digits, haemorrhagic blisters → bone scan / angiography

4Diagnosis & Classification

Classification

Degree Findings Newer class / prognosis
1st Central white area + surrounding erythema Superficial – good
2nd Clear/cloudy blisters within 24 h Superficial – good
3rd Haemorrhagic blisters (painless) / black eschar Deep – poor
4th Tissue necrosis Deep – poor

Key radiology findings

Tc-99m bone scanassess severity: 1st at day 2 (absent uptake = poor prognosis, not necessarily necrosis); 2nd at day 5

Day-5 blood/bone pool Action
Normal Expectant
Diminished Observe ± early debridement
Absent Early debridement / amputation; tPA candidate

MRI T2↑ signal in necrotic muscle; not the initial test

5Management

Frostbite
  • Field→pad/splint, prevent refreezing; rewarm only if warmth can be maintained
  • ED→warm IV fluids, tetanus, NSAIDs, RAPID REWARM 40-42°C water bath
    • <24 h, no flow on bone scan, 2nd/3rd degree→IV tPA
  • Necrosis → wait for demarcation (1-3 mo)→LATE DEBRIDEMENT / AMPUTATION

Prevention – insulated footwear

Most reliable preventionthermal insulation footwear / reduce shoe heat loss (toes: little muscle → little heat)

✗ Wrong options: Distractors — hard-soled shoes (comfortable shoes ✓), industrial toe-caps, compression stockings, high-protein diet, warm drinks, triple socks, carbo-loading

Rewarming

Water bath40–42°C; 30 min (Orthobullets) · 15–30 min (Golant); mild antibacterial

End pointskin pliable and red-purple

Avoid 50°C → thermal burn · lower temp → ↓ survival · avoid freeze-thaw cycles

Hypothermia rewarmingmild: external (passive/active; active → "afterdrop") · moderate/severe: internal core (warm O₂/IV, lavage, bypass, CAVR ~1°C/15 min); avoid alcohol/sedatives

Acute treatment – blister care & thrombolysis

Blister Management
Clear (superficial) Debride + topical aloe vera (↓ PGF2α, TXB2)
Haemorrhagic (deep) Drain/aspirate, leave skin intact → prevents dermal desiccation
Intact Leave, dry gauze

Liquid nitrogen finger, haemorrhagic blisterdrain, leave roof intact
✗ Wrong options: HBO · full debridement + flap · MRI · wet-to-dry

IV tPA (tissue plasminogen activator)within 24 h → ↓ digital amputation; indication: no flow on bone scan, 2nd/3rd degree
✗ Wrong options: superficial

Unconscious in snow, cold blue digits, no cap refill, 2PD >15 mmtPA
✗ Wrong options: diltiazem · amlodipine [Raynaud's] · collagenase [Dupuytren] · diclofenac

tPA contraindications
General Alcoholic (head injury bleed), active bleeding, ICH/surgery <3 mo, concurrent trauma, major surgery <14 d, aneurysm/AVM, bleeding diathesis, pregnancy, labile HTN
Cold-related >24 h cold exposure, warm ischaemia >6 h, multiple freeze-thaw

Other adjunctsLMW dextran, anticoagulants; HBO anecdotal; IV Abx only if infected

Rehabwhirlpool hydrotherapy, PT/OT

Delayed debridement/amputation after demarcation

Timingafter demarcation, 1–3 months → "frostbite in January, amputate in July"
✗ Wrong options: days · weeks

Before demarcation, no sepsismoist dressings + observation (like burns; much may be superficial)

Immediate surgery onlyescharotomy (circumferential constriction) · fasciotomy (compartment syndrome)

Sympathectomy↓ pain duration + time to demarcation; no ↓ extent of necrosis

6Complications

Adult Detail / treatment
Persistent pain 50% (intolerable 15%)
Cold intolerance —
Vasospasm Raynaud's, colour change, hyperhidrosis → CCB, vasodilators, β-blockers, late sympathectomy
Neuropathy ↓ NCV → decompression (CTR)
Frostbite arthropathy Subchondral bone loss, osteopenia, contractures DIP > PIP → arthroplasty
Child Detail
Premature physeal closure 1–2 y after exposure (chondrocyte injury)
Late (>10 y age) Joint laxity, angular deformity, short digits, excess skin, DJD → physeal arrest, osteotomy, arthrodesis

Severity ↑alcohol intoxication, skin contact with metal/ice, high wind chill

Chilblain Trench foot Frostnip Frostbite
Freezing No No Yes Yes
Wet/dry Dry Wet — —
Tissue loss No ± No (reversible) Yes

Wall All arterial layers, true endothelial lining No endothelial lining

DBI Meaning / action

Operative criteriaDBI <0.7 · thrombosis with aneurysm · ischaemia multiple digits · recurrent symptoms after nonop

Aneurysmalways surgical: excision of segment + reconstruction ± vein graft → prevents emboli, removes painful mass, relieves ulnar nerve, removes vasospasm trigger

Acute <1 mo Thrombosis (patency 98% → <88% in 1st month)

Not failure causes at 6 mograft resorption, recurrent aneurysm, hamate nonunion compression, thrombosis (acute only)

Interpreting NCS in carpal tunnel syndrome

Abnormal for CTS (Orthobullets NCS note)distal sensory latency >3.2 ms · motor latency >4.3 ms

Mild–moderate CTS↑ latency + ↓ NCV, normal amplitude = focal demyelination, axon number intact

Severe/chronic CTS↓ amplitude (SNAP/CMAP) = axonal loss from ischaemia → surgery less predictable

Prognosismild–moderate + temporary relief from steroid injection → CTR predictably relieves

EDS in CTSnot needed for diagnosis; only EDS grades mild → severe; ambiguous cases, outcome prediction

SNAP vs CMAPsensory nerve action potential vs compound motor action potential

Peripheral Nerve Injury & Repair

Hand · 60 / 103

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence16.9 / 100,000 / yr; 2.6% of UE trauma, 1.2% of LE trauma; ~3% of UE/hand injuries

Demographics♂ 80%, age 32–39

Risk factorspenetrating / high-energy trauma, crush, displaced fractures

Commonest UE nerve injury (OB)ulnar nerve, working-age males

Nerve microanatomy (epineurium, perineurium, endoneurium)

Layer Covers Function / MCQ fact
Epineurium Group of fascicles → whole nerve Cushions against external pressure; collagen + elastin; focus of surgical repair
Perineurium Individual fascicle Tensile strength + elasticity; blood–nerve barrier; limits diffusion (protects from oedema)
Endoneurium Individual axon (+ Schwann cell, myelin) Forms Schwann cell tube; nourishes axon; must be intact for full recovery
Myelin Axon Schwann cells; ↑ conduction velocity; saltatory at nodes of Ranvier

Cross-section labels (OB)A axon · B myelin · C epineurium · D perineurium · E endoneurium · F node of Ranvier

✗ distractorsfibronectin/laminin (ECM, directional branching), N-cadherin (adhesion, growing axons)

Neuroncell body <10% of mass (metabolic centre); axon conducts; dendrites receive

Blood supplyextrinsic vessels in loose tissue + intrinsic plexus in epi-, peri-, endoneurium

Fibre types

Fibre Diameter Myelin Speed Carries
A 10–20 µm Heavy Fast Touch (Aβ)
Aδ Thin Myelinated Medium-fast Pain + temperature (TO) — sharp, first pain
B <3 µm Moderate Medium Autonomic
C <1.3 µm None Slow Pain — dull, delayed (TO)

Sensory receptors

Receptor Adaptation Senses Test
Merkel Slow Pressure, texture, low-freq vibration Static 2PD
Meissner Rapid Light touch Moving 2PD
Pacinian Rapid High-freq vibration, rapid indentation (~1 mm ovoid) Vibration
Ruffini Slow Skin stretch

2Mechanism

Stretch8% elongation → ↓ microcirculation 50%; 15% → ↓ 80%; e.g. stingers, suprascapular n. in volleyball, CPN after TKA valgus correction

Compression30 mmHg → paresthesia, ↑ latency; 60 mmHg → complete conduction block; endoneurial oedema → fibrosis → ↓ gliding

Chronic compressionconduction change from Schwann cell proliferation + apoptosis; Schwann cells ↑ VEGF
✗ Wrong options: Wallerian degeneration · axon transection · cell body apoptosis

Compressive neuropathy (cubital tunnel, NCV 31 m/s)neurapraxia of ischaemic origin
✗ Wrong options: axonotmesis · endoneurial disruption

Lacerationsharp better than crush; ends retract

Classic injury Nerve
Anterior shoulder dislocation Axillary
Holstein-Lewis (distal 1/3 humerus), Saturday night palsy, extension SCH Radial
Distal humerus ORIF, flexion SCH, OR positioning Ulnar
Extension SCH, prominent olecranon TBW pins (anterior ulnar cortex) AIN
Posterior hip dislocation Sciatic
TKA valgus correction CPN
Percutaneous tibial plating, holes 11–13 Superficial peroneal

Regeneration physiology

Wallerian degenerationdistal to injury (TO); axoplasm + myelin degraded by phagocytes; proximal reaction = primary/retrograde degeneration (TO)
✗ Wrong options: Schwann cells

Sequencedistal Wallerian → Schwann cells proliferate, line basement membrane → proximal budding after ~1 month → antegrade growth 1 mm/day
✗ Wrong options: distal → proximal · neurotrophic factors direct phagocytosis

Advancing Tinel~1 inch/month (TO); most reliable sign of recovery

Guidancecontact guidance (Schwann basal lamina), neurotropism, neurotrophic factors

Order of recoverysympathetic → pain → temperature → touch → proprioception → motor; loss in reverse; motor first lost, last to return

Myelindisrupted before axon

3Presentation

Diagnosisclinical (injury + deficit); EMG/NCS mainstay; exploration confirms traumatic injury

Radial palsy (Holstein-Lewis) last to recoverwrist extension
✗ Wrong options: elbow extension: spared at this level

4Diagnosis & Classification

Injury classification (Seddon / Sunderland)

Seddon Sunderland Damaged Wallerian Tinel advances Recovery
Neurapraxia 1 Focal demyelination (ischaemia); axon intact No No (no motor march; simultaneous proximal + distal recovery) Complete, days–6 wk
Axonotmesis 2 Axon; endo-, peri-, epineurium intact Yes Yes Full (intact endoneurial tube)
Axonotmesis 3 Axon + endoneurium; peri-/epineurium intact Yes Yes Most variable, incomplete
Axonotmesis 4 Axon + endo- + perineurium; only epineurium intact Yes No Neuroma-in-continuity; poor without surgery
Neurotmesis 5 All layers (transection) Yes No None without repair
— 6 (Mackinnon) Mixed degrees in one nerve Mixed; neuroma in continuity (TO)

Sunderland 2 = axon disrupted, endoneurial tube intact (TO); regeneration because endoneurium intact
✗ Wrong options: epineurium, perineurium, myelin, Schwann cell

Tinel progressionSunderland II & III (TO)

Neurotmesis rangeSunderland 5 (Orthobullets classification) · 3rd–5th (Orthobullets treatment section, OB214026) — read the options

Full recovery prevented byendoneurial injury = neurotmesis (structure A in figure)

Key radiology findings

High-resolution USdynamic, superficial nerves; localises entrapment, cut ends, neuromas

MRI / MR neurographybrachial plexus; better for muscle denervation, deep structures, static resolution

Sensory receptors & electrodiagnostics

Study Finding Meaning
NCS ↑ latency, ↓ velocity, ↓ SNAP/CMAP Large myelinated fibres; compression/demyelination
EMG Fibrillations, positive sharp waves Acute denervation (axonotmesis / neurotmesis)
EMG Fasciculations, myokymia Neurogenic
EMG CRDs, myotonic discharges Myopathy
Polyphasic MUPs Early reinnervation (TO)
Chronic MUPs (large amplitude, long duration) Established reinnervation (TO)
↓ SNAP & CMAP Axonal loss (quantitative) (TO)
↓ / absent insertional activity Poor potential for surgical reinnervation (TO)
↓ recruitment Loss of innervated MEPs (TO)

ThresholdsDSL >3.2 ms, DML >4.3 ms abnormal; velocity <52 m/s (Orthobullets) · <50 m/s across elbow (OB); amplitude ↓ 50% vs contralateral

SNAPs affected before CMAPs; EMG normal until late

Cubital tunnel NCSprolonged distal sensory latency + ↓ velocity
✗ Wrong options: fibrillations, PSW, fasciculations = EMG · ↑ velocity

NeurapraxiaNCV slowing/conduction block, no fibrillations

EMG valueoften only objective evidence (workers' comp)

5Management

Nerve deficit
  • Closed injury / neurapraxia / Sunderland 1–2→observe + serial EMG (baseline 3–4 wk)
    • no recovery by 3 mo→explore
  • Sharp / iatrogenic / vascular injury / progressive→early exploration + repair (7–14 d)
  • Gunshot with transection→repair at 1–3 wk (zone of injury declares)
Gap after resecting to healthy fascicles
  • Tension-free→primary epineurial (or fascicular) repair
  • Small sensory gap (≤20 mm)→collagen conduit / processed allograft
  • >5 cm or motor/mixed→autograft (sural; cable if size mismatch)

Surgical repair

Repair windowbest 7–14 d; unpredictable after 6 mo; reinnervation by 18 mo goal; time limit 18 mo

Epineurial repairresect proximal neuroma + distal glioma to "mushrooming" fascicles; align with epineurial vessels; tension-free; gain length by transposition/neurolysis

Fascicular repairperineurial sutures; outcome = epineurial; ↑ scarring; matching by topography, stimulation (proximal: sensory in awake pt; distal: motor before Wallerian), histology

Direct muscular neurotizationstump into muscle; ↓ neuroma; TMR, RPNI for amputees

Timing of repair after ballistic injury

GSW with transected radial nervedefinitive repair 1–3 wk after injury
✗ Wrong options: at initial debridement · at fracture fixation · after 3 mo · wait for neuroma

GSW without transection / closed humerus fractureobserve 3 mo (mostly neurapraxia); GSW brachial plexus → observe

Repair options – conduit, allograft & autograft by gap length

Option Gap Key facts
Collagen conduit ≤20 mm (Orthobullets, OB) · <3 cm (OB4644) · tubular wrap <1 cm (OB219234) Type I collagen (= ligaments; not cartilage/NP II, basement membrane IV, vessels III); relies on fibrin clot; nutrient + neurotrophic access; 8 mm digital gap → as good as autograft (✗ Wrong options: PGA, GTMC, silicone, end-to-end under tension)
Decellular allograft Sensory <3 cm; effective up to 7 cm Scaffold (microtubules, laminin) for host Schwann cell migration; no living cells, no immunosuppression; not yet for motor/mixed
Non-processed allograft Needs immunosuppression — rarely used
Vein conduit Digital not >5 cm, not superior
Autograft >5 cm (50 mm) Gold standard; graft ≥10% longer than gap; sural (palm level), MABC, LABC, terminal PIN; cable for mismatch; donor morbidity

Quality of recoverydrops with gaps >5 mm

Segmental defect, motor recoverynerve autograft best
✗ Wrong options: allograft, conduits, vein

Prognosis – nerve, level & order of recovery

Favourableyounger age (most important), distal level (2nd), sharp / stretch injuries

Unfavourableolder age, proximal level, crush/blast, delay, ulnar nerve, concomitant bone/soft-tissue injury, graft length

Best motor recovery after graft (<6 mo)radial
✗ Wrong options: median, ulnar, tibial, peroneal

Ulnarpoor outcomes (worse than tibial, radial, femoral, MC)

✗ Wrong options: Prognostic factor — type of autograft (sural vs saphenous); ✓ time to repair, level, length, rehab

High median laceration + 6 cm sural cable graft — poorest recoverythumb opposition (intrinsics; endplates survive ~12 mo)
✗ Wrong options: wrist flexion, finger flexion, FPL, sensation

Bone Nonoperative Operative
P1 & P2 Extra-articular <10° angulation, <2 mm shortening, no rotation; undisplaced intra-articular >10° angulation, >2 mm shortening, any rotation, displaced intra-articular, unstable/irreducible, grossly contaminated open

Criterion

Bilateral involvement

5Management

Raynaud's
  • First line→stop smoking + avoid cold + biofeedback + medication
    (CCB, topical nitrate, ASA, sildenafil …)
  • Failed medical Rx, ischaemia/pain (± ulcer)→botulinum toxin A (off-label)
  • Severe / impending gangrene / ischaemic ulcer→periarterial (digital) sympathectomy ± arterial reconstruction
    • segmental occlusion of one major artery→microvascular reconstruction

Medical management

Criticalsmoking cessation + avoid cold; thermal biofeedback; stress, protective garments

Commonest drugcalcium channel blocker (nifedipine; oral only)

Other drugsASA, sildenafil / PDE inhibitors, intra-arterial reserpine, dipyridamole, pentoxifylline, prostaglandins, ACE-I/ARB, TCAs, SSRIs, α-antagonists

Topical vasodilator mechanism

Topical nitrateonly topical drug used; ↑ cGMP in vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation

Not topicalNSAID (COX), steroid (PLA2), lidocaine (Na⁺), CCB (L-type Ca²⁺ — oral only)

Botulinum toxin – mechanism, outcomes & pre-treatment testing

Indicationfailed medical management + ischaemia/pain; ulcers not a contraindication; off-label

Mechanismcleaves pre-synaptic SNAREs → ↓ ACh release → ↑ digital perfusion

Other proposedblocks α2 receptor recruitment on vascular smooth muscle · ↓ substance P & glutamate (pain) · inhibits RhoA kinase → ↓ smooth-muscle constriction · may ↓ sympathetic tone

Outcomesall of: ulcer healing, ↓ pain, ↓ cold intolerance, ↑ digital blood flow

Absolute contraindicationspregnancy / breastfeeding → urine pregnancy test before injection · anaphylactic allergy · active infection · aminoglycosides / anticholinergics

Cautionrespiratory disease, myasthenia gravis

✗ Wrong options: Traps — proprioception (non-depolarising blockers), Ca²⁺ channel excitability (gabapentin/pregabalin), muscle strengthening

Periarterial sympathectomy indications

IndicationRaynaud's failed medical Rx + ischaemic digital ulcer / impending gangrene; esp. collagen vascular / occlusive disease

Techniqueperiarterial (digital) = commonest; strip adventitia + sympathetic fibres; may extend to forearm

Not indicatedcalcific arterial disease · Buerger's in active smoker · CRPS (stellate block instead) · diabetic Charcot · TOS

Thoracoscopic sympathectomyout of favour → rebound hypersympathetic response

Microvascular reconstructionrare: small-segment occlusion of one major artery, other spared

Digital ischaemiaulceration, gangrene → amputation

Modality Fact

Scaphoid nonunion

Situation Treatment

Scaphoid Lunate Advanced Collapse (SLAC)

1Basics

SL dissociation – pathomechanics

Definitionpredictable degenerative arthritis from chronic SL dissociation; most common form of wrist arthritis (Watson & Ballet 1984)

CausesSL ligament tear (most common cause of carpal instability); also crystalline arthropathy

SLILC-shaped: dorsal, proximal (fibrocartilage), volar; dorsal = thickest (3 mm) & strongest → most critical for SL stability (volar ~1 mm)

Not key SL stabilisersRSC (sectioning with intact SLIL → no kinematic change), DRC, DIC, volar SLIL

SL dissociationscaphoid flexes + lunate extends = DISI; SL angle >70°, lunate >10° extended

Why radiolunate sparedlunate stays concentric in spheroidal lunate fossa in all positions of rotation

2Mechanism

Stages & sequence of arthritis (radial styloid, radioscaphoid, capitolunate; radiolunate spared)

Sequenceradial styloid–scaphoid → entire radioscaphoid → capitolunate (capitate migrates proximally into SL gap, subluxes dorsally on lunate)

First joint affectedradioscaphoid (radial styloid tip)

Sparedradiolunate (and lunotriquetral)

3Presentation

Symptomspain at SL interval, difficulty weight-bearing through wrist, stiffness, progressive weakness

Signsdorsal SL tenderness, ↓ ROM, ↓ grip

Watson scaphoid shiftpressure on scaphoid tuberosity, wrist ulnar → radial deviation → scaphoid subluxes dorsally (pain) → clunk on release; positive early only (arthritis stabilises scaphoid later); compare sides

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsPA + lateral; stress views and MRI unnecessary for staging

SL diastasis (PA)>3 mm (Orthobullets) · >2 mm + asymmetric to other side (OB) — read the options

PA by stageI: radial styloid beaking, sclerosis · II: narrowing whole scaphoid fossa · III: capitolunate narrowing, capitate migrates proximally

LateralDISI, capitate subluxed dorsally on lunate

MRIthinning of proximal scaphoid / scaphoid facet / capitolunate cartilage, synovitis

Watson classification

Stage Arthritis Image
I Radial styloid – scaphoid
II Scaphoid – entire scaphoid facet of radius
III Capitate – lunate (+ scaphocapitate)
"IV" (controversial) Radiolunate / pancarpal —

Radiolunate sparedall Watson stages; pancarpal ("stage IV") → think other aetiology (RA, AVN)

DifferentialSNAC (stage II = scaphocapitate; proximal pole preserved as extension of lunate)

5Management

SLAC wrist
  • Mild→NSAIDs, splint, steroid injection
  • Stage I→radial styloidectomy / AIN + PIN denervation
  • Stage II→PRC or scaphoid excision + 4CF
    (smoker / fewer complications → PRC)
  • Stage III (capitolunate)→scaphoid excision + 4CF or wrist fusion
  • Radiolunate / pancarpal→total wrist fusion

Procedure Needs intact Contraindicated by
PRC Radiolunate facet + capitolunate (capitate head) + RSC Capitolunate arthritis (stage III), incompetent RSC
Scaphoid excision + 4CF (capitate–lunate–triquetrum–hamate) Radiolunate facet Radiolunate arthritis
Total wrist fusion — — (best pain relief + grip, loses motion)

Not contraindicationsradioscaphoid arthritis, capitolunate arthritis (for 4CF), SL disruption, scaphoid osteonecrosis

Radial styloidectomyopen or arthroscopic (1-2 portal); removes scaphoid–styloid impingement

DenervationPIN + AIN (distal branches = proprioception/capsule only) ± dorsal ulnar sensory, radial sensory, LABC, palmar cutaneous; ↓ pain, no ↑ function/strength/ROM; can add to bony procedures for II–III

Salvage – four-corner fusion vs PRC (capitolunate arthritis contraindication, RSC ligament)

PRCexcise scaphoid + lunate + triquetrum; capitate sits in lunate fossa; preserve RSC = primary stabiliser after PRC (prevents ulnar translocation)
✗ Wrong options: DRC, DIC, ulnocapitate, ulnotriquetral

4CF + scaphoidectomymotion through radiolunate joint; only option addressing all stage III sites

PRC vs 4CF (stage II)similar long-term results; PRC = fewer complications, technically easier, no prolonged immobilisation → preferred in smokers (Tomaino)
✗ Wrong options: nonunion, hardware, dorsal impingement

Not for SLACSTT fusion (SL instability, STT OA, Kienböck) · scaphocapitate fusion (Kienböck) · distal pole excision (SNAC) · RSL fusion · TWA (young/active, e.g. farmer; OK for older low-demand / RA)

Total wrist fusionpancarpal / radiolunate arthritis, failed PRC; less suitable in a 65-year-old needing motion

RSL fusionradioscaphoid + radiolunate OA with preserved midcarpal joint

Add distal scaphoid pole excision (~20%)↑ ROM (dart-thrower's motion), ↓ strain → ↑ fusion rate; ± triquetrum excision

Without itnonunion, poor motion (esp. radial deviation), weak grip

Scaphoid excision + 4-corner fusion (or capitolunate arthrodesis) Stage II–III (incl. capitate arthritis) Retains 60% motion, 80% grip

RSC ligamentmost volar-radial ligament; radial styloid → carpus obliquely, radial to long & short RL ligaments → excision at PRC → ulnar translocation of carpus

Definitiondisplaced distal phalanx physeal fracture + nailbed injury in children (TO) = open fracture

FDPinserts volar metaphysis → flexion force on shaft

Anatomy & management – nail bed repair, remove interposed tissue, reduce

Open Seymournail plate removal + nailbed repair + removal of interposed soft tissue (germinal matrix) + open reduction

Must includeremoval of interposed soft tissue (pinning optional adjunct)

Pinning (conflict)open reduction + retrograde K-wire across fracture + DIPJ (Orthobullets, Abzug) · pinning not required; nail plate replaced under fold = sufficient stability (OB)

Avoid DIPJ-sparing pinpoor purchase in epiphysis

Avoid closed reduction + pin in interposition → locks germinal matrix in fracture

Avoid mallet splint in situ / buddy tapinggrowth & nail disturbance

Nailbedrepair every nailbed injury; absorbable (6-0) suture or Dermabond

Open vs closedopen management fewer complications; Abzug: surgery for open and closed

ED management89% managed in ED; OR mainly for failed closed reduction (Lin)

Antibioticswithin 24 h → infection 6.9% vs >24 h → 76.5% (Rask; overall 27.3%); clindamycin for delayed (bone penetration)

Grade Findings Tear

    • failed / arthritic→MCP fusion 15° flexion

Nonoperative (4–6 wk; TO partial: spica 4 wk) Operative repair
Partial tear (unstable in flexion only) Complete tear (unstable flexion + extension)

Not a surgical indication (TO)ipsilateral metacarpal fracture

UCLS/chevron incision; transosseous sutures / anchors; immobilise IP free; strength 4–6 wk; >90% excellent; RTP ~100%

Debridement1A; 3-4 + 6R portals; keep 2 mm peripheral rim; 80% pain relief; not effective with ulnar-positive variance

Repair1B–1D (peripheral, vascular); acute athletic best; outside-in / inside-out / transosseous; immobilise 6 wk; acute (<3 mo) → 80% motion + grip; risk ECU tendonitis (knot), dorsal sensory nerve

Amsterdam wrist rules (X-ray criteria)

X-ray if any Suspected distal radius # Suspected carpal #
↑ age, swelling, deformity, TTP distal radius Pain on palmarflexion, supination, painful radioulnar ballottement; pain on ulnar deviation = ↓ risk Male, snuffbox swelling, pain on radial deviation; painful thumb axial compression = ↓ risk

Key radiology findings – views

View Position / beam Best for
AP / PA Shoulder abd 90°, elbow 90°; supinated (AP) / pronated (PA) Carpal joints: AP > PA; DRF
Lateral Shoulder adducted, elbow 90°, forearm neutral; 10° cephalad Alignment, carpal instability; adequate = pisiform volar cortex within central 1/3 of volar scaphoid
IR oblique (pronated 45°) Radial carpus; best for scaphoid waist + distal pole
ER oblique (supinated 45°) Ulnar carpus; pisiform, hamate body
Ulnar deviation Aim at scaphoid Scaphoid #, lateral wrist; scaphoid/lunate extend
Radial deviation Medial wrist, palmar triquetral #; scaphoid/lunate flex
Carpal tunnel Wrist extended; 2.5 cm distal to MC3 base, 25–30° cephalad Hook of hamate (best), pisiform, trapezium
Carpal bridge 4 cm proximal to wrist bend, 45° caudad Pisiform, trapezium, hamate hook
Clenched fist Supinated, ulnar dev, fist (capitate driven proximally); bilateral SL injury
Scaphoid view 30° extension + 20° ulnar deviation Scaphoid #
Clements-Nakayama Pronated 45°, ulnar dev; at snuffbox (20° cephalad if can't deviate) Trapezium #

Scaphoid fracture

Location %
Waist 65
Proximal 1/3 25
Distal 1/3 10 (commonest in children)

PAproximal pole; waist/distal pole distorted (scaphoid flexed)

Negative X-ray + high suspicionthumb spica, repeat X-ray 14–21 d (re-evaluate 12–21 d)

ORIF criteria (instability) Threshold
Displacement >1 mm any view
Humpback 15°
SL angle >60°
Radiolunate angle (DISI) >15°
Intrascaphoid angle >35°
Other Proximal pole, perilunate, comminuted, vertical/oblique unstable, non-displaced waist (listed)

Lunate / perilunate dislocation

PAbreak in Gilula's arc, lunate–capitate overlap, piece-of-pie

Lateralloss of radius–lunate–capitate colinearity; stage III capitate dorsal to lunate; stage IV spilled teacup; SL angle >70°

Timing Treatment
Acute <8 wk Emergent closed reduction/splint → open reduction, ligament repair, fixation ± CTR (✗ Wrong options: nonop)
Chronic >8 wk PRC
Chronic + degenerative Total wrist arthrodesis

Fracture Best view Nonop Surgery
Triquetrum Lateral / IR oblique (dorsal); radial dev (palmar) Stable dorsal/palmar cortical, undisplaced body ORIF if unstable / displaced body
